pages.name: Arrows that keep their line
pages.text: A matrix usually knocks an arrow off its own line. Along a few directions it only stretches or squishes the arrow. Take `A = [3 1; 0 2]`. The probe `(0, 1)` gives `(1, 2)`, which points somewhere else. Along `(1, 0)`, Av is `(3, 0)`. That is 3 lots of v, so the line lights and `λ = 3`. Along `(−1, 1)`, Av is twice v, so `λ = 2`. Such an arrow is an [[eigenvector]]. λ is its [[eigenvalue]], the factor it is stretched by.
pages.alt: A pane with the probe arrow v on its circle and the arrow Av. v is ( minus 0.71, 0.71) and Av is ( minus 1.41, 1.41). v’s line is lit, λ equals 2.

pages.name: Which keeps its line?
pages.task: For `A = [3 1; 0 2]`, which arrow stays on its own line?
pages.why: `(−2, 2)` is 2 lots of `(−1, 1)`, so it lies on the lit line. `A(−2, 2) = (−4, 4)`, which is still 2 lots. Each eigenvector is really a whole line of them, because any multiple works too. That whole line is the [[eigenspace]] for `λ = 2`.
pages.alt: A pane with the probe arrow v on its circle and the arrow Av. v is ( minus 2, 2) and Av is ( minus 4, 4). v’s line is lit, λ equals 2. A( minus 2, 2) equals ( minus 4, 4), still 2 lots.

pages.name: A flip keeps the line
pages.text: A negative λ flips an arrow but keeps it on its line. The mirror `[0 1; 1 0]` swaps an arrow’s two numbers. It keeps `(1, 1)` as it is, so `λ = 1`. It turns `(1, −1)` into `(−1, 1)`. That points the opposite way along the same line, so `λ = −1`.
pages.alt: A pane with the probe arrow v on its circle and the arrow Av. v is (0.71, minus 0.71) and Av is ( minus 0.71, 0.71). v’s line is lit, λ equals minus 1.

pages.name: A matrix with no lit line
pages.task: Which keeps no line at all: the shear, the quarter turn or the mirror?
pages.why: The quarter turn turns every arrow through 90°. So Av is always square to v and never on its line. Its equation is `λ² + 1 = 0`, which has no real root. The shear has `λ = 1` twice, yet only one line, through `(1, 0)`.

pages.name: The grid goes flat
pages.text: `Av = λv` becomes `(A − λI)v = 0`. Here I is the matrix that leaves every arrow alone. So v is a nonzero arrow that `A − λI` crushes to zero. That happens only when its grid lies flat, with area scale 0. So `det(A − λI) = 0`. This is the [[characteristic equation]]. At `λ = 2` it lies flat, as `(3 − 2)(2 − 2) = 0`. It crushes the line through `(−1, 1)`. At `λ = 3` it crushes the line through `(1, 0)`.

pages.name: Why λI?
pages.task: Why write `(A − λI)v = 0` and not `(A − λ)v = 0`?
pages.answer: A matrix minus a number means nothing
pages.why: You cannot take a number from a matrix. So write λv as λIv. That is the same arrow, because I leaves every arrow alone. λI has λ down its diagonal. So `A − λI` takes λ off each diagonal entry.

λI keeps λ a whole number

pages.name: Trace and determinant
pages.text: The eigenvalues add up to the [[trace]], the sum of the diagonal. They multiply to the determinant. For `[a b; c d]`, `det(A − λI)` is `(a − λ)(d − λ) − bc`. That is `λ² − (a + d)λ` `+ (ad − bc)`. With roots p and q, it is also `(λ − p)(λ − q)`, or `λ² − (p + q)λ + pq`. Matching the two gives both rules. `B = [2 −1; −1 2]` has trace 4 and determinant 3. So `λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0`, and λ = 1 or 3.

pages.name: The other eigenvalue
pages.task: `[4 1; 2 3]` has one eigenvalue 5. What is the other?
pages.why: The eigenvalues add up to the trace, `4 + 3 = 7`. So the other is `7 − 5 = 2`. They also multiply to the determinant. `4 × 3 − 1 × 2 = 10`, and `5 × 2 = 10`.
pages.alt: A pane with the probe arrow v on its circle and the arrow Av. v is (0.45, minus 0.89) and Av is (0.89, minus 1.79). v’s line is lit, λ equals 2. 5 + 2 equals 7, the trace.

pages.name: Each direction
pages.text: To find each direction, put each λ back. For `λ = 1`, `B − I = [1 −1; −1 1]`. Both rows say `v₁ − v₂ = 0`. So v is `(1, 1)`, or any multiple. For `λ = 3`, every entry of `B − 3I` is −1. Its rows say `v₁ + v₂ = 0`, so v is `(1, −1)`. One row is enough, because at an eigenvalue the other is a multiple of it. As a check, `B(1, −1) = (3, −3)`, 3 lots of `(1, −1)`.
pages.alt: A pane with the probe arrow v on its circle and the arrow Bv. v’s line is not lit. B minus I equals [1 minus 1; minus 1 1], so v₁ minus v₂ equals 0. B minus 3I equals [ minus 1 minus 1; minus 1 minus 1], so v₁ + v₂ equals 0.

pages.name: A zero answer
pages.task: Take `A = [3 1; 0 2]` and `λ = 3`. Someone’s working ends at `v = (0, 0)`. What does that tell them?
pages.answer: There is a slip in the working
pages.why: `A − 3I = [0 1; 0 −1]`. Its rows say `v₂ = 0` and nothing about v₁. So it crushes the whole line through `(1, 0)`. Here λ = 3 is right, so the slip is in solving the rows. v₁ is free, so `v = (1, 0)` works. The zero arrow never counts, because `A0 = λ0` for every λ.

pages.name: Three lines in space
pages.text: A 3 by 3 matrix gives a cubic in place of the quadratic. Take `C = [1 1 0; 1 2 1; 0 1 1]`. Expanding `det(C − λI)` gives `−λ³ + 4λ² − 3λ = 0`. It has no plain number term, so `λ = 0` is a root. The rest gives λ = 1 or 3, as for B. Three lines light. `(1, −1, 1)` goes with 0, `(1, 0, −1)` with 1 and `(1, 2, 1)` with 3. The line for 0 is C’s [[null space]].

pages.name: Mixed: the eigenvalues
pages.why: The trace is `5 + 2 = 7`. The determinant is `5 × 2 − 2 × 2 = 6`. So `λ² − 7λ + 6 = 0`, which is `(λ − 1)(λ − 6) = 0`. Reading 5 and 2 off the diagonal works only when every entry on one side of the diagonal is 0.

pages.name: Mixed: the pairs
pages.task: `[5 2; 2 2]` has eigenvalues 1 and 6. Which pairing is right?
pages.why: Each eigenvector goes with the λ you put in to find it. `A(2, 1) = (12, 6)`, which is 6 lots of `(2, 1)`. `A(1, −2) = (1, −2)`, which is 1 lot of `(1, −2)`.
